guide.title: Brighton Beach, Brooklyn: Little Odessa on the Boardwalk
guide.intro: William A. Engeman began building a beach resort here in 1868, and in 1878 Henry C. Murphy and his fellow investors gave the development its name, borrowed from the English seaside city of Brighton. The Brighton Beach Hotel and Bathing Pavilion opened that same year, reached by the Brooklyn, Flatbush and Coney Island Railway, an excursion line that opened on July 2, 1878. When erosion threatened the hotel a decade later, the whole 5,000-ton building was jacked up and moved 495 feet inland in April 1888 on hydraulic jacks and railroad cars. The hotel closed in 1924, four years after a tunnel under Flatbush Avenue linked the BMT Brighton Line to the Broadway subway in Manhattan and turned a rail-excursion resort into a subway neighborhood. From the mid-1970s Soviet Jewish emigres settled here in numbers, and the nickname Little Odessa followed.

sections.heading: From resort to Little Odessa
sections.body:
Wikipedia calls the 1888 relocation of the Brighton Beach Hotel the largest building relocation of the nineteenth century. It was a rescue operation: the sea had eaten far enough into the beach to threaten the building, so contractors put the whole thing on jacks and rails and moved it back from the water. The hotel lasted until 1924.

By then the neighborhood's future was already decided. The BMT Brighton Line's subway connection through a tunnel under Flatbush Avenue opened on August 1, 1920, and the year-round residents who arrived by subway displaced the summer crowd who had arrived by excursion train.

Soviet Jewish emigres, predominantly Ashkenazi Jews from Russia and Ukraine, began settling here in the mid-1970s, and the large number from Odessa gave the neighborhood its nickname. A second wave followed the collapse of the Soviet Union in 1991. The result is the commercial strip under the elevated tracks on Brighton Beach Avenue, where the restaurants and bakeries below run to Georgian, Uyghur and Turkish cooking.

Hurricane Sandy hit hard in October 2012. A February 2016 report by the Brighton Neighborhood Association, LISC and the Hester Street Collaborative recorded up to fifteen feet of sea and sewer water in parts of the neighborhood and described recovery as still incomplete three years on.

sections.heading: Getting there
sections.body:
Brighton Beach station, over Brighton Beach Avenue between Brighton 5th and Brighton 7th Streets, is the neighborhood's station. The Q serves it at all times. The B serves it on weekdays only — rush hours, middays and early evenings — originating and terminating here on the inner express tracks.

Ocean Parkway station sits at Brighton Beach Avenue and Ocean Parkway, on the border of Brighton Beach and Coney Island. The Q stops there at all times; the B does not stop there at all.

No NYC Ferry landing serves Brighton Beach. A Coney Island-area route was postponed indefinitely as of 2022 because of site and engineering problems, with the Economic Development Corporation reported to be restudying feasibility in late 2025.

sections.heading: Where the lines fall
sections.body:
Neighborhood boundaries here are not fixed by any authority, and different sources draw them differently. The 2016 Brighton Neighborhood Association report describes Brighton Beach as bordered by Coney Island to the west at Ocean Parkway, Manhattan Beach to the east at Corbin Place, Gravesend to the north at the Belt Parkway, and the Atlantic Ocean to the south at the Riegelmann Boardwalk. That is one description among several and should not be read as a settled line.

The uncertainty is not academic. Century Playground, which is commonly listed as a Brighton Beach park, is recorded by NYC Parks at 2955 West 3 Street in zip code 11224 — a Coney Island address, on a West-numbered street rather than a Brighton-numbered one. It sits in Coney Island. Asser Levy Park, likewise often attached to Brighton Beach, is placed by Wikipedia between Surf Avenue and Sea Breeze Avenue, streets generally associated with Coney Island and Sea Gate, and which neighborhood it falls in is not settled.

faq.question: How do I get to Brighton Beach?
faq.answer: By Q train at all times to Brighton Beach station, over Brighton Beach Avenue between Brighton 5th and Brighton 7th Streets. The B also serves it on weekdays during rush hours, middays and early evenings, originating and terminating there. Ocean Parkway station, on the border with Coney Island, is served by the Q only.

faq.question: Does the B4 bus serve Brighton Beach?
faq.answer: No. The B4 runs between Bay Ridge, at Narrows Avenue and 77th Street, and Sheepshead Bay, at Knapp Street and Voorhies Avenue, via Bay Ridge Parkway, Stillwell Avenue, Neptune Avenue and Shore Parkway/Emmons Avenue — none of which run through Brighton Beach. It is sometimes listed as a Brighton Beach route, but its own route description does not support that.

faq.question: Why is Brighton Beach called Little Odessa?
faq.answer: For the large number of immigrants from Odessa among the Soviet Jewish emigres who settled here from the mid-1970s, mostly Ashkenazi Jews from Russia and Ukraine. A further wave arrived after the Soviet Union collapsed in 1991.

faq.question: Where can I eat in Brighton Beach?
faq.answer: On Brighton Beach Avenue: Brighton Güllüoğlu at 239 for Turkish baklava and pastry, Cafe Kashkar at 1141 for Uyghur cooking, Berikoni / Georgian House at 125, and Ocean View Cafe at 290. Off the avenue, Tatiana is at 3152 Brighton 6 Street and Geo Khinkali at 3071 Brighton 4 Street.

faq.question: Is Cafe at Your Mother-in-Law's still open?
faq.answer: No. 3071 Brighton 4th Street is now occupied by Geo Khinkali, a different Eastern European restaurant. Georgian House has also moved: it now operates as Berikoni / Georgian House at 125 Brighton Beach Avenue rather than at its former Brighton 1st Street address.

faq.question: Where can I stay in Brighton Beach?
faq.answer: None is listed here, and no hotel from a neighboring neighborhood is substituted for one. The Sheepshead Bay and Manhattan Beach pages list no lodging either.

places.name: Brighton Beach
places.address: Along the Riegelmann Boardwalk, Brooklyn, NY 11235
places.summary: The city-maintained public oceanfront that fronts the neighborhood, operated by NYC Parks and contiguous with Coney Island Beach to the west along the same barrier peninsula.

places.name: Brighton Playground
places.address: 126 Brightwater Court, Brooklyn, NY 11235 (Brighton 2nd Street between Brightwater Court and the Boardwalk)
places.summary: An NYC Parks playground built in 1950 and renovated in the late 1990s. Brighton Playground is the official NYC Parks name; it is often listed as Brighton Beach Playground.

places.name: Grady Playground
places.summary: An irregular parcel between Shore Parkway and Brighton 3rd and 4th Streets, classified by NYC Parks as a jointly operated playground.
places.history: The city acquired the site on May 7, 1942.

places.name: Babi Yar Triangle
places.address: Brighton 14th Street, Corbin Place and Ocean View Avenue, Brooklyn, NY 11235
places.summary: A small NYC Parks traffic triangle dedicated in 1981 in memory of the Babi Yar massacre and renovated in 1988. It is a memorial rather than a destination park.

places.name: Brighton Güllüoğlu
places.summary: A Turkish baklava and pastry cafe on the main commercial strip under the elevated tracks.

places.name: Cafe Kashkar
places.summary: A Uyghur restaurant on Brighton Beach Avenue.

places.name: Berikoni / Georgian House
places.summary: A Georgian restaurant on Brighton Beach Avenue. It carries the same name that once traded as Georgian House at 129 Brighton 1st Street.

places.name: Geo Khinkali
places.summary: An Eastern European restaurant at the Brighton 4th Street address that was previously Cafe at Your Mother-in-Law's.

places.name: Tatiana
places.summary: A Russian-cuisine restaurant near the boardwalk, at 3152 Brighton 6 Street, though often listed as Tatiana Grill at a Brighton 4th Street address.

places.name: Ocean View Cafe
places.summary: An Eastern European cafe on Brighton Beach Avenue.
